content.thinking:
The leak inflates offline metrics but doesn't touch what users actually see, so it explains the offline/online gap without being the true source of the regression — something else, like capacity, mixture, or lr_scale, is genuinely hurting online quality. The fact that learning rate has never been re-tuned after model size changes hints that lr_scale mismatched to the new scale could be the real culprit.

This time capacity was reduced while lr_scale was raised to 1.295 without retuning — that mismatch could destabilize the smaller model in a way offline greedy decoding masks but online sampling exposes, since sampling amplifies overfitting or sharp-minima behavior that greedy decoding smooths over. Normally offline and online numbers should track closely, so a big divergence points to something sampling-sensitive breaking, consistent with lr/capacity mismatch. I also note the new data source added this quarter with an open overlap audit could be a separate confound.

I'll test lr_scale reset first since it's cheapest, using canary for validation. Before executing lab calls, let me double-check the budget state — the spec call showed budget_left at 20.0, suggesting no calls have been consumed yet this session, so I should confirm that before proceeding.

With a full budget of 20 untouched, I'm mapping out a careful plan: first decontaminate the release config to gauge leak magnitude, then rerun with leak explicitly set to zero for a clean baseline comparison, and consider canary tests on individual knobs to isolate the true cause while watching my remaining budget.

Given the hints pointing to lr_scale interacting with capacity as the likely culprit, I'll prioritize a cheap canary test resetting just lr_scale before confirming with capacity and mixture. Following the R2 counterfactual logic, I need two configs: one resetting lr_scale alone (expecting recovery near 0.87) and one holding lr_scale at release while resetting capacity and mixture (expecting the regression to persist near 0.74) — this gives me the two canary tests needed to confirm lr_scale as the cause.

Estimating costs, the lr_scale-only canary runs at base rate (4/rep) while the capacity+mixture canary incurs the multiplier (6-8/rep), totaling around 11 for one rep each. I'm also considering running a full-reset canary (all three knobs at their allowed limits) to establish the maximum reachable online performance, which matters for judging whether recovery hits the 90% threshold — this also carries the multiplier since capacity/mixture are changed. Given the note that lr has never been re-tuned after model size changes, I suspect lr_scale is the true single cause and the capacity/mixture shifts are incidental, so I want to verify this by also testing capacity reset alone with lr_scale held at release.

I'm also confirming that our 20-unit budget is only for our own investigation, separate from whatever hidden re-runs the grader performs, so I want to plan for using roughly 14-16 units for a confident diagnosis with margin left over. My plan is to start with a single-rep canary changing only lr_scale (cost 4), keeping capacity and mixture at release values, as the first diagnostic step.

Then I'd try a second canary that resets capacity and mixture toward their release values while holding lr_scale fixed, to test whether lr_scale alone is the cause—if regression persists, that strengthens the case. Depending on results I might need individual tests for capacity or mixture alone, but before spending more budget on canaries, I want to cheaply pull decontamination info first, since it's low-cost and could clarify the leak situation without extra canary runs.

content.thinking:
Resetting both capacity and mixture together, with lr_scale held at the release value, recovers online performance to 0.8058 — a substantial jump from 0.7411 toward the original 0.8705, roughly 50% recovery. That's meaningful but not complete, and the cost came in at 9, higher than the expected estimate.

With only 6 budget left, I can't safely run a single-knob canary (capacity alone or mixture alone) since each could cost 6-9. Instead I should use decontaminate, which has a flat cost of 1 regardless of knob type, to test capacity alone and mixture alone as a cheaper proxy for disentangling their individual contributions.

Reviewing what I have: the release baseline, the lr_scale-only reset (no change, ruling out lr_scale as the cause), and the capacity+mixture reset together (which recovered about half the online score). This confirms lr_scale isn't the driver, and now I need to isolate whether capacity or mixture (or both) is the true cause behind the recovery, spending the remaining budget carefully on decontaminate tests for each knob individually.
